e.t: This Hebrew noun means “horns,” referring to the projecting parts of an animal. In the Old Testament, it is also used for horns connected with worship objects and for horns mentioned in speech or imagery. Its exact force—whether one horn or more—comes from the sentence and context. The word occurs 76 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it represents a recurring biblical term rather than a rare expression.

This Hebrew word means “murmured,” describing low or complaining speech directed against someone or in response to a situation. It portrays people expressing dissatisfaction rather than speaking openly with grateful or trusting words. The word occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in Deuteronomy, Psalms, and Isaiah. In Deuteronomy, it functions as the predicate describing Israel’s complaint against the LORD; in Isaiah, it is connected with people whose understanding is changed. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “proud,” describing someone or something marked by pride. It is rare in the Old Testament, appearing three times: twice in Job and once in Isaiah. The repeated rendering in Job supports “proud” as its clearest ordinary sense, while the Isaiah occurrence shows that the word’s precise force can depend on the surrounding sentence. It should therefore be understood as a word expressing pride, with context determining how that quality is presented.

e.t: The Hebrew word refers to “Lehi,” a named place in the Old Testament. It appears twice in the Hebrew corpus, both in Judges 15:17, and functions as a place-name rather than an ordinary description or action. Its longer lemma is associated with the same name, while the English rendering preserves “Lehi.” The surrounding verse supplies the historical significance of the location; this word itself identifies the place.

This Hebrew word means “flame.” It names the visible, fiery form of fire when Scripture describes what is seen. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Daniel: once in Daniel 3:22 and once in Daniel 7:9. Its central meaning remains focused and concrete: a flame is the burning appearance associated with fire, rather than an action or a person. The surrounding verse determines the specific scene in which the flame appears.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “ignorance,” especially something done “unwittingly”—without conscious knowledge or intention. It describes a person’s lack of awareness in an action, rather than deliberate rebellion or planned conduct. The word appears 19 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, particularly in Leviticus and Numbers, where it helps distinguish inadvertent wrongdoing from intentional acts. Its use in Ecclesiastes also connects this condition with speech and action before God. The precise force in any verse depends on its surrounding context.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “cease.” It is used as a verb, expressing that an action or condition stops or comes to an end. Its five Old Testament occurrences appear in Genesis, Numbers, Esther, and Jeremiah, showing use across several kinds of biblical writing. In Esther 2:1, it functions as the predicate connected with the king and wrath, showing how it can describe an intense condition coming to an end.

The word means “heaven,” referring to the realm or expanse above the earth. In these Hebrew Scriptures, it describes what is above and the heavenly sphere connected with God’s revelation and rule. It occurs 38 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in Daniel and Ezra. The word may describe heaven as the realm above or as the place from which heavenly matters are revealed. Its precise force in any individual verse comes from the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “drink.” It functions as an action word, describing the act of taking liquid. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalm 102:9. The word’s basic sense is simple and concrete: it identifies drinking rather than a person, place, object, or abstract idea. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its ordinary lexical meaning remains the action of drinking.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “dragons,” naming a creature in the Old Testament. It appears 26 times across 26 verses, beginning in Genesis and continuing through Micah. Its uses include creation language and descriptions involving serpentine or threatening creatures, so the surrounding passage determines the specific picture intended. The word functions as a name for the creature itself rather than an action or quality. It is also associated with the creature addressed in Ezekiel’s speech concerning Egypt’s ruler.
